full_judgment:
K. M. Subhan, J.—This Rule was issued at the instance of Defendant Petitioners Nos. 1 and 2 against whom a suit has been filed by the Plaintiff opposite party being Money Suit No. 4 of 1969 seeking a decree for Tk. 1,96,62, 28,255. The defendant petitioners are body, corporates being incorporated in the State of Delaware having principal offices of business at East Hartford, Connecticut in the United States of America. The defendant petitioners filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge before whom the suit was pending, under Order 7 rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This application was filed on 18.3.70.

Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate has next contended that the Courts in Bangladesh has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit in view of clause (4) of Article 6 of the contract entered into between the parties. Alternatively, the learned Advocate has argued that the suit may be stayed to enable the parties concerned to refer the matter to arbitration. In support of this contention Mr. Hafizullah has submitted that clause 4 of Article 6 ousts the jurisdiction of the Courts in Bangladesh and his second contention is, that if any cause of action has arisen, in the matter of the accident as alleged by the plaintiff opposite party, it has arisen in U.S.A. where the helicopters were manufactured and as such no cause of action has arisen in this country, and as such the suit is not maintainable in the court of this country. In this regard Mr. Hafizullah has also submitted that the Courts shall always be reluctant to pass a decree which could not be executed and the decree of the courts of Bangladesh are not executable in U.S.A. and as such the plaint should be rejected. In so far as, the first point of the learned Advocate is concerned, namely, ouster of Jurisdiction by clause 4 of Article 6, it is necessary to look into the clause itself which is in the following terms:— 

 8. We have ascertained from Mr. Altaf Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite Party, if they are willing to refer the matter to arbitration because there is no arbitration clause as admitted by Mr. Hafizullah himself in the agreement signed between the parties in the contract. Mr. Altaf Hossain has submitted that the plaintiff opposite party is not agreeable to any arbitration. Arbitration, being a matter between the disputing parties to the contract and is dependent upon their intention to have the dispute determined in a quasi-judicial manner by arbitrators we find that the plaintiff opposite party cannot be forced to go to arbitration in the absence of arbitration clause in the agreement, Next, we come to the question of passing an ineffective decree as submitted by Mr. Hafizullah as there being no reciprocal agreement between Bangladesh and U.S.A. Reference in this connection may be made to sections 13 and 44 (a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 13 provides conclusiveness of foreign judgment in so far as the courts of this country are concerned. Section 14 (a) speaks of execution of the decree passed by courts in the United Kingdom and other reciprocating territory. These two sections, if read together, clearly point out that there is no bar in the Municipal Courts of this country to entertain a suit and pass a decree which is likely to be executed in a foreign country other than the United Kingdom. All that section 44(a) lays down is that there must be reciprocal agreement between this country and the foreign concern. There is nothing in the record of this case and nor has anything been produced before us by either party, to show that there is reciprocal agreement or the absence thereof. In this view of the matter we do not find any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate Mr. Hafizullah either.
